results.summary: This design implements a six-bit roulette that lights one of six 7-segment display segments in sequence. A chain of six flip-flops holds a single 'ball' bit that advances on each clock cycle, with reset loading the ball into the first flip-flop. It is tested by setting the clock to 10 Hz, pressing reset to light segment A, and observing the light spin around the display. The project requires an external 7-segment display and is a simple Wokwi-based educational design.

This is a two-bit adder built from AND, OR and XOR gates that computes A + B + Cin = S with Cout. The eight inputs and eight outputs are exposed on the Tiny Tapeout pins, and the truth table in the documentation describes all eight input combinations. It is tested by applying input values and observing the sum and carry outputs. The design is a straightforward educational arithmetic circuit with no external hardware required.

This project claims to implement a riddle but provides no explanation of what the riddle is or how the circuit works. The pins expose two inputs, a and b, and two outputs, and and nand, suggesting a simple combinational logic block. The documentation explicitly defers both the explanation and test procedure to a later time. Because the description is essentially empty, the design cannot be evaluated beyond its pin names.

This project is titled 'title' with the one-line description 'addieren', suggesting a binary adder that drives a 7-segment display. The pins include two inputs, a and b, and seven segment outputs a through g, but the documentation consists only of placeholder letters. There is no usable explanation of the logic or test procedure. The design is effectively undocumented and its behaviour cannot be determined from the provided text.

This design uses a state machine built from flip-flops to display the text TUAN9304 on a 7-segment display. The documentation includes a full state table mapping each state to segment outputs and next-state logic, cycling through characters including blanks and a decimal point. It is tested by pressing reset to initialise state 0 and observing the repeating sequence on the display. The project requires an external 7-segment display and is a Wokwi-based educational exercise.

This project has a temporary title and the one-line description 'Nothing currently', with pins for two inputs and a single XOR output. The documentation states that it currently does not work and that there is no test procedure. No external hardware is listed. The design is essentially an empty template and cannot be meaningfully described beyond its XOR pin name.

This project is a four-bit counter built from D flip-flops, with outputs labelled output0 through output3. The documentation admits that it does not work yet and that the author has no idea how to test it. No external hardware is specified. Because the design is incomplete and undocumented, its intended behaviour can only be inferred from the title and pin names.

This project is described as a full single-bit adder with inputs a, b and c and outputs a, b, c and d. The documentation states plainly that it does not work and cannot be tested. No external hardware is required. The design is non-functional and the pin naming is inconsistent, so no reliable behaviour can be confirmed.

This design converts a four-bit binary input into a single-digit 7-segment display output, accepting values from 0 to 9. The four input pins are ordered with pin 0 as the least significant bit and pin 3 as the most significant bit. It is tested by entering any number on the inputs and observing the corresponding digit on the display. The project requires one external single-digit 7-segment display and is a simple Wokwi-based BCD exercise.

This is a very simple clock divider that toggles two outputs, out6 and out7, at a divided rate from the 100 Hz input clock. The documentation gives no detail on the division ratio or internal structure beyond calling it primitive. It is tested by applying a 100 Hz clock and releasing reset, with the outputs intended to drive segment G and the decimal point of a digit indicator. The design requires an external 7-segment display and is a basic educational Wokwi project.
